newsitem.title: USA: Alaska ferry siege highlights salmon industry woes.
newsitem.headline: Alaska ferry siege highlights salmon industry woes.

text.p: Canadian fishermen's three-day siege of an Alaskan ferry did more than escalate tensions with the U.S. over salmon quotas, it highlighted woes of the entire industry -- a worldwide glut and eroding prices.

Low prices have stoked the fires in longstanding disputes between the two neighbours over Pacific salmon allocations that erupted in this week's blockade of the Alaskan ferry Malaspina, said Bob King, press secretary for Alaska Gov. Tony Knowles.

"Right now the industry is under considerable economic stress, and I think that is one of the underlying factors that is fuelling this thing," King said. "It has made the question of who's catching whose fish even more pointed."
In 1988, three years after the Pacific Salmon Treaty was signed, prices were at a peak.
Salmon from southwestern Alaska's Bristol Bay -- site of the world's biggest sockeye run -- fetched nearly $3 a pound then. Now, Bristol Bay sockeyes are bringing little more than 50 cents a pound.

Sockeyes from Alaska's Copper River, considered a premium product, were selling recently for 80 cents a pound, down from the $1.55 offered at the start of the season in May, according to state figures.
Prices for all species of salmon, from all regions, have taken similar dives.

Production of farmed salmon, minimal in 1980, has boomed and now accounts for over 40 percent of world salmon output, displacing wild and hatchery salmon in the market, according to state figures. Salmon farming is illegal in Alaska, but huge natural runs have produced record harvests in recent years here.
Glut-induced low prices are only one factor in the complicated issue of salmon allocation, said Gunnar Knapp, a University of Alaska Anchorage economist specialising in fishery issues.

"I think low salmon prices generally increase the level of tension in the industry, but Canadians are still going to be upset about the perceived U.S. interception of fish, regardless of price," Knapp said.

The ferry blockade resulted from Canadian anger over Alaskans' alleged interception of an estimated 400,000 sockeye salmon bound for British Columbia's Skeena River, a run experiencing a high return this year. Alaskans say the catches are unintentional and occur while fishermen are targeting Alaska's abundant Noyes Island pink salmon run.
For Alaskans, state ferries, all named for noted Alaska glaciers and dubbed "blue canoes", are vital to transporation in southeast Alaska, where almost all towns lack road access.
Prince Rupert, the British Columbia port where the blockade was staged, may suffer as a result of the siege.
Alaska suspended the Prince Rupert ferry service when the blockade started Saturday and is considering cancelling it entirely, King said.
"The value of the (Alaska) Marine Highway System calling into the Prince Rupert economy is $72 million a year," said Tom Garrett, director of the Alaska Division of Tourism.
On Tuesday, Prince Rupert Mayor Jack Mussallem sent a letter of apology to Knowles and asked for ferry service to resume.

Alaska Attorney General Bruce Botelho said the state plans to sue blockaders for lost state revenues, including lost ferry bookings and refunds paid to passengers who left the Malaspina while it was stuck in Prince Rupert.
More than business was affected, said Kim Elton, a state legislator from Juneau. Also held up in the blockade was a travelling version of the Vietnam War memorial, he said.
"I think there was a lot of resentment that the Vietnam War veterans wall was held hostage in this," Elton said.
